short_summary: Chronic diseases, including cardiovascular, metabolic, and neurodegenerative disorders, are heavily driven by a self-perpetuating cycle of oxidative stress and chronic inflammation. This comprehensive review delineates the core molecular mechanisms underpinning this oxidative-inflammatory axis, focusing on the interplay between reactive oxygen species (ROS) and key redox-sensitive signaling pathways such as NF-κB and Nrf2. While ROS act as critical signaling molecules at physiological levels, their dysregulation promotes persistent pathological signaling. The article evaluates current methodologies for quantifying oxidative stress biomarkers, including lipid peroxidation products, protein carbonyls, and DNA oxidation markers like 8-OHdG. It also critically analyzes the paradoxical failure of conventional, non-targeted antioxidant clinical trials, attributing these shortcomings to the disruption of essential ROS signaling and poor bioavailability. To overcome these limitations, the review highlights emerging precision medicine strategies, including mitochondria-targeted antioxidants like MitoQ, Nrf2 activators, nanotechnology-based delivery systems, and multimodal therapies targeting sirtuins and immunometabolism.
long_summary:
This whitepaper provides an in-depth analysis of the oxidative-inflammatory axis, a fundamental pathological mechanism driving chronic diseases such as cancer, cardiovascular disorders, and neurodegeneration. At the core of this axis is the bidirectional relationship between reactive oxygen species (ROS) and pro-inflammatory signaling. ROS, generated by endogenous sources like the mitochondrial electron transport chain and NADPH oxidases, serve as essential signaling molecules under normal physiological conditions. However, chronic oxidative stress activates the NF-κB pathway, which induces the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines that, in turn, stimulate further ROS production. Conversely, the Nrf2-Keap1 pathway acts as a master regulator of the cellular antioxidant defense, orchestrating the expression of cytoprotective genes to restore redox homeostasis. The article explores the intricate cross-talk between these pathways, emphasizing that their dysregulation fuels disease progression.

Furthermore, the review details standardized methodologies for quantifying oxidative damage across cellular macromolecules, highlighting biomarkers such as malondialdehyde (MDA), F2-isoprostanes, protein carbonyls, and 8-OHdG. Despite robust preclinical evidence linking oxidative stress to disease, conventional non-targeted antioxidant therapies, such as high-dose vitamin E, have consistently failed in clinical trials. The text attributes this antioxidant paradox to the oversimplification of redox biology, poor compound bioavailability, and the unintended disruption of physiological ROS signaling.

To bridge this translational gap, the article advocates for precision redox medicine. It details advanced therapeutic strategies, including mitochondria-targeted antioxidants like MitoQ, which utilize lipophilic cations to accumulate directly within the mitochondrial matrix. Additionally, it explores the use of nanotechnology-based delivery systems, such as lipid nanoparticles and polymeric carriers, to enhance the stability and targeted delivery of antioxidant compounds. The review also highlights emerging therapeutic targets, including sirtuins, immunometabolic modulators, and biomimetic redox enzymes. By integrating biomarker-guided patient stratification, multi-omics approaches, and synergistic combination therapies, researchers can develop more effective interventions to disrupt the vicious cycle of oxidative stress and inflammation.
